A 14-year-old female adoles-
cent was managed in our department. She had been treated for several months for
drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy an d gradually presented major anterograde
amnesia with confusion. Upon her arrival at the University Hospital Centre, she showed
a classical form of stiff person syndrome. The brain magnetic resonance imaging
showed bitemporal hyperintensities and hypertrophy of the amygdala. The blood and
cerebrospinal ﬂuid were positive for GAD65 antibodies. At 2 years of immunosuppres-
sive treatment and rehabilitation, the course showed partial improvement of the
memory and neuropsychiatric impairment, and epilepsy that continued to be active.
GAD65 antibodies are associated with various neurological syndromes, and this
presentation combining limbic encephalitis and stiff person syndrome is the ﬁrst
pediatric form published to date; there are also few cases described in adults.

The patient is a 14-year-old girl with normal psychomotor
development born to nonblood-related parents. The family
history includes Hashimoto’s thyroiditis in several aunts, and
she had a personal history of depigmented vitiligo skin lesions.
She started by presenting with focal seizures that
were secondarily generalized and were treated by lamotri-
gine. These seizures were stereotypical and began with a
sensation of nausea, disorientation and confusion, and chew-
ing. After several weeks of progression and lamotrigine
treatment, she gradually showed memory impairment
with antegrade amnesia and recurrent episodes of loss of
contact. Her epilepsy quickly became drug-resistant, and
there was no cognitive improvement despite the changes in
treatment. The assessment done up till then included
electroencephalography (EEG) that did not describe a frank
focus, and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain
described as normal.
Three months after the start of care, the patient had painful
lumbar stiffness with subacute onset and abdominal spasms.
The physical examination identi ﬁed stiff person syndrome
(SPS), abdominal contraction, and considerable psychomotor
slowing and anterograde amnesia with gradual forgetfulness.
The general laboratory tests were normal except for in-
creased creatine phosphokinase at 603 IU/L. Serology testing
did not show recent viral infection, and the viral polymerase
chain reactions were negative in the CSF (cytomegalovirus,
Epstein–Barr virus, human herpesvirus-6, varicella-zoster vi-
rus). CSF testing showed normal cellularity, protein level that
was also normal, 3 to 10 oligoclonal bands, and positive result
for GAD65 antibodies (indirect immuno ﬂuorescence, ref.
504225, Inova Diagnostics, San Diego, United States, and
immunodot, ref. PNS9DIV-24, Ravo Diagnostika, Freiburg,
Germany). The blood was also highly positive for GAD anti-
bodies at over 2000 IU/L (RSR GADAb ELISA, ref. GDE/96, RSR
Limited, Pontprennau, United Kingdom). Review of the initial
MRI identiﬁed T2 bitemporal hyperintensities and hypertro-
phy of the amygdala (
►Fig. 1.1 ); the follow-up cerebrospinal
MRI could not be interpreted due to abnormal movements. The
EEG video showed a bitemporal intercritical focus with little
activity, noncortical myoclonus, and sleep/wake physiological
organization. The CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
found no suspicious neoplastic mass, and the positron emis-
sion tomography scan only found nonpathological increased
uptake of the esophagus and stomach, diagnosed 3 months
later as herpes esophagitis.
The patient was admitted to our department and we began
a treatment with sequential courses of intravenous cortico-
steroids (1 g per day for 5 days) and polyvalent immunoglo-
bulins (1 g/kg/day for 2 days) every 3 weeks for 4 months. The
antiepileptic treatment was replaced by zonisamide.
She received care at the rehabilitation center between
treatment courses and hospitalizations. After 3 months of
treatment, there was mild improvement, but severe memory
impairment and active signs of epilepsy continued. The GAD65
antibodies were still greater than 2000 IU/L in the serum and
CSF. The MRI showed marked improvement in the inﬂamma-
tion signs but the start of atrophy of the amygdala. Due to these
factors, a decision was made for a second line of treatment
with rituximab (2 doses of 375 mg/m

2) combined with two
supplementary courses of corticosteroids and immunoglobu-
lins. An overall follow-up assessment at 1 year of disease
progression found epilepsy still active on zonisamide and
oxcarbazepine, mild internal temporal atrophy on MRI
(
►Fig. 1.2 ), and CSF still positive for antibodies, with high
levels in the blood. The rituximab was continued every
6 months with a good CD19 and CD20 depletion, but also a
decrease in gamma globulins necessitating supplementation.
The latest year of follow-up showed no improvement on
memory, an epilepsy stable with 1 crisis per months with
sodium valproate and lacosamide, but recurrent psychotic
episodes of 24 hours every 2 weeks and a progressive stiffness
recurring. There was no decrease in the GAD65 antibodies in
blood and CSF, and the MRI shows now a cortical and subcor-
tical atrophy (
►Fig. 1.3 ). Recently, we decided to intensify the
treatment with rituximab and cyclophosphamide.
Fig. 1 Coronal T2 cerebral magnetic resonance imaging showing (A) at diagnosis bitemporal hyperintensities and hypertrophy of the amygdala,
(B) after 3 months of treatment an atrophy of the amygdala and (C) at 2 years follow-up cortical and subcortical atrophy.

There are considerable memory sequelae, with an overall
memory index score on the Children’s Memory Scale that had
not improved since the start of care, stable at 50/100, that
is, less than 0.1 percentile for age ( ►Supplementary Table S1
[online only]). Progress had only been made on visual memory
and facial recognition, with no improvement in verbal memory
abilities (►Supplementary Fig S1 [online only]).

This case associated with the diagnosis of GAD encephalitis
and SPS is, to our knowledge, the ﬁrst case described in a
child. This illustrates the variability of neurological syn-
dromes associated with these antibodies, 2 including in chil-
dren, despite the few cases known to date.
